videos.desc:

Omar Bradley spent World War One guarding copper mines in Montana while his classmates went to France. Twenty-eight years later he commanded four American armies, and history gave the credit to louder men.

He was the farm boy from Missouri who worked as a railroad boilermaker for seventeen cents an hour, graduated in the middle of West Point's "class the stars fell on," and did not see combat until he was fifty. videos.title: Montgomery’s Top 3 Genius Moves | The General Who Ended Germany’s Winning Streak
videos.desc:
#Montgomery #WW2 #MilitaryHistory

Bernard Montgomery beat Rommel in the desert and commanded every Allied soldier on the ground in Normandy. By January 1945, America's leading field general was telling Eisenhower he could not serve under him.

He was vain, tactless, and maddeningly slow, and the Americans who fought beside him never forgave his habit of taking the credit. But the record tells a story his critics rarely finished. videos.desc:
Erwin Rommel was the general his enemies admired most. In October 1944, the regime he served handed him a capsule of poison, then gave him a state funeral and blamed his wounds.

The British spent two years saying his name with something close to awe. Their commander in the Middle East ordered his officers to stop calling him a magician. Their Prime Minister called him "a great general" in the House of Commons while the war was still undecided. videos.title: George S. Patton's Top 3 Legendary Tactical Moves
videos.desc:
In August 1943 George S. Patton struck two soldiers in Sicilian field hospitals and was nearly finished as a commander. On D-Day he was in England, the figurehead of an army that did not exist. Nineteen months after the slapping incidents, he put a regiment across the Rhine before Montgomery, for a few dozen casualties.

videos.title: Heinz Guderian's Top 3 Legendary Tactical Moves | Fired for Being Right
videos.desc:
Heinz Guderian broke the French Army in 1940 and helped trap an entire Soviet army group in 1941. On Christmas 1941, he was sent home in disgrace for pulling his freezing soldiers back from ground they could not hold.

He was a signals officer who did not sit inside a tank until 1929. By 1937 he had written the book on armoured warfare. In May 1940 his panzers crossed the Ardennes, a forest the French high command called impenetrable, and forced the Meuse at Sedan in 57 hours. Six days later they were standing on the English Channel.

videos.desc:

George Washington lost more major battles than he ever won, and in the winter of 1777 his own officers were whispering about replacing him. Four years later he trapped a British army at Yorktown and won the war.

In the summer of 1776 the largest expedition Britain had ever sent overseas came ashore at New York. Washington's army was outflanked at the Jamaica Pass, pinned against the East River at Brooklyn Heights, and chased the length of New Jersey.
